question: I feel sick. Where should I go first?
expected_answer: Student Health, Medical Care, 3535 Market St, Suite 100. Call 215-746-WELL (9355) to book. True emergency: 911, or PennComm 215-573-3333 on campus.

question: Do I have to go to Student Health first?
expected_answer: Yes, for most non-emergency care if you are within 25 miles of campus. Without a Student Health referral, care is paid at the Non-Preferred level with a $1,500 deductible.

question: Student Health is closed. Where do I go?
expected_answer: Call 215-746-WELL (9355); a provider is on call 24/7 and will tell you where to go. No referral is needed when Student Health is closed.

question: It's Saturday night and I have a high fever. What should I do?
expected_answer: Call 215-746-WELL (9355) for the on-call provider. If it feels like an emergency, call 911. The bot does not judge how serious it is.

question: Should I go to urgent care or the ER?
expected_answer: Urgent care for problems that can't wait but aren't life-threatening; ER for true emergencies, not mild illness. If unsure, call the on-call provider at 215-746-WELL.

question: Which urgent care near campus takes PSIP?
expected_answer: Penn lists examples (not endorsements): Vybe Urgent Care Center City, Jefferson Urgent Care at Rittenhouse, Jefferson Urgent Care at Washington Square. Check Aetna's provider search for network status.

question: Which hospital near campus should I go to in an emergency?
expected_answer: Penn Medicine ERs: HUP (1 Convention Ave), Penn Presbyterian (51 N. 39th St), Pennsylvania Hospital (800 Spruce St). In an emergency, the nearest ER.

question: I need a dentist. Where do I go?
expected_answer: PSIP covers only injury to natural teeth and impacted wisdom teeth. For routine dental care, buy the Penn Student Dental Plan or the Aetna Student Dental Plan.

question: I need an eye exam or glasses. Where do I go?
expected_answer: Annual eye exams need no referral. Adult eye exam: plan pays 90% in network, 60% out of network, no deductible, 1 exam per year. Glasses or contacts: plan pays 100% up to $125 per year; contact lens fitting visits are not covered. Optional Aetna Vision Preferred plan ($65 per year): exam $10 copay, $130 frame allowance.

question: I want to see a therapist. Where do I start?
expected_answer: Counseling at 3624 Market St, First Floor West. Drop in during hours or call 215-746-WELL (9355) any time. Outside mental health care needs no referral.

question: How do I see a specialist?
expected_answer: Book a Student Health visit first; the provider sends a referral before your specialist appointment.

question: Can I see a doctor online?
expected_answer: Yes. Telemedicine visits are covered the same as in-person visits: $35 copay for a doctor or specialist, $10 copay for mental health. The PDFs do not name a specific Aetna 24/7 virtual care service.

question: Is there a nurse I can call for advice?
expected_answer: Yes: 215-746-WELL (9355), 24/7, connects to Student Health's on-call provider.

question: Do I need a referral to see a specialist?
expected_answer: Yes, if you are within 25 miles of Student Health and none of the exceptions apply.

question: How do I get a referral from Student Health?
expected_answer: See a Student Health provider; they send the referral to the outside provider before your appointment.

question: How long is a referral valid?
expected_answer: Until July 31, the end of the plan year.

question: Do I need a new referral for a follow-up visit?
expected_answer: Not in the same plan year for the same condition. A new referral is needed for each condition each plan year.

question: Do I need a referral for urgent care or the ER?
expected_answer: Not for an emergency, not when Student Health is closed, and not more than 25 miles away. Urgent care while Student Health is open and you are within 25 miles: yes. Urgent care is not a referral exception, so without one the visit is paid at the out-of-network level (plan pays 70% after the $1,500 deductible).

question: Do I need a referral for mental health care?
expected_answer: No. Inpatient and outpatient mental health and substance use care are exempt.

question: I'm more than 25 miles from campus. Do I still need a referral?
expected_answer: No.

question: What happens if I see a doctor without a referral?
expected_answer: The claim is paid at the Non-Preferred level, with a $1,500 deductible, so you pay much more.

question: Is a Student Health visit free?
expected_answer: Visits are covered by the Clinical Fee ($385 per semester), which all full-time students pay. Some items, like labs sent to an outside lab, are billed to insurance.

question: What does the Clinical Fee cover?
expected_answer: Access to Student Health and Counseling as your primary care provider. Most routine medical care and all counseling are covered; some services, tests, medications or treatments may be billed to insurance or cost extra. The full list is not published.

question: Will my blood test cost money?
expected_answer: It may. Labs sent to an outside lab are billed to your insurance. Outpatient labs need no referral. At an in-network lab you pay a $35 copay; at an out-of-network lab the plan pays 70% after the deductible.

question: How much is an urgent care visit with PSIP?
expected_answer: $35 copay in network, no further cost. Out of network: plan pays 70% after the deductible. Non-urgent use of urgent care is not covered.

question: How much is an ER visit with PSIP?
expected_answer: $100 copay per visit, no deductible. Out-of-network ERs are paid the same as in network. The copay is waived if you are admitted. Non-emergency use of the ER is not covered. No referral needed for emergencies.

question: How much does a specialist visit cost?
expected_answer: With referral: $35 copay per visit. Without referral: paid at the out-of-network level (plan pays 70% after the $1,500 deductible).

question: How much will an X-ray or MRI cost?
expected_answer: X-ray and lab work: $35 copay. MRI, CT or PET scan: $50 copay. Out of network: plan pays 70%. Whether an MRI needs prior authorization is not stated; check Aetna's online precertification list.

question: Do vaccines or TB tests cost extra?
expected_answer: Student Health gives flu shots, travel vaccines and all Penn-required vaccines. PSIP covers preventive vaccines at 100% in network; vaccines needed for travel or work are not covered. Wellness has said extra fees may apply for vaccines. TB test cost is not published.

question: Is birth control covered?
expected_answer: Yes. Student Health offers gynecologic and sexual health care; reproductive health needs no referral. Generic and over-the-counter birth control is $0 at in-network pharmacies, up to a 12-month supply; brand-name methods are $0 when no generic exists. Contraceptive counseling is covered at 100% (2 visits per year).

question: Is therapy covered, and for how many sessions?
expected_answer: Counseling at Student Health is covered by the Clinical Fee. Outside therapy needs no referral: $10 copay per visit in network, no deductible, telemedicine included. No session limit is listed. Out of network: plan pays 70%.

question: What is my deductible?
expected_answer: $400 in network (with a referral) and $1,500 out of network (including care without a referral), per person per year. Many services skip the deductible, including preventive care, the ER, prescriptions, mental health and vision.

question: What's the most I could pay in a year?
expected_answer: The out-of-pocket maximum is $1,500 per person ($3,000 per family) in network, and $4,000 per person ($8,000 per family) out of network. The two totals are counted separately.

question: What happens if I go to an out-of-network doctor?
expected_answer: The plan pays 70% after the $1,500 out-of-network deductible, with a $4,000 out-of-pocket maximum. The doctor may bill you the difference (balance billing), except where the No Surprises Act protects you; in emergencies you only owe your normal share.

question: How do I make an appointment at Student Health?
expected_answer: Call 215-746-WELL (9355). After your first visit you can book online in PennChart.

question: Can I walk in without an appointment?
expected_answer: Counseling: yes, during business hours. Medical Care: not stated.

question: What are Student Health's hours during breaks and summer?
expected_answer: Normal hours: Mon–Wed 9 am–7:30 pm; Thu 10 am–6 pm; Fri 9 am–5 pm; Sat 10 am–3 pm; Sun closed. Break hours are posted in an alert bar on the Wellness site. Phone line is 24/7.

question: How do I book a first appointment at CAPS?
expected_answer: CAPS is now Counseling at Student Health and Counseling. Call 215-746-WELL (9355) any time or drop in at 3624 Market St.

question: What should I bring to my appointment?
expected_answer: Your Aetna insurance card (printed or in the Aetna Health app), a photo ID, your list of medicines and allergies, and your referral details if seeing an outside provider.

question: Where do I find my insurance card and member ID?
expected_answer: Print it from the Aetna Student Health website, or open it in the Aetna Health app.

question: The clinic asked if I have insurance. What do I tell them?
expected_answer: "I have Aetna Student Health through the Penn Student Insurance Plan," and show the card. Mention your Student Health referral if you have one.

question: The clinic wants me to pay upfront. Is that normal?
expected_answer: In-network clinics often collect the copay at the visit; the rest is billed after Aetna processes the claim. Aetna does not pay out-of-network providers directly, so they may ask you to pay in full. Keep the itemized receipt and send Aetna a claim form within 90 days.

question: The doctor wants to send my test to an outside lab. Will I be charged?
expected_answer: Possibly. The lab bills your insurance: a $35 copay if the lab is in Aetna's network, more if it is not (plan pays 70% after the deductible). Ask which lab it is and check it is in Aetna's network.

question: Is my medication covered?
expected_answer: Look the drug up in the 2026 Aetna Pharmacy Drug Guide (Advanced Control Plan, Aetna Student Health PA). Each drug has a tier: PG preferred generic ($20), PB preferred brand ($50), NP non-preferred ($75), PSP or NPSP specialty, and NF not covered unless an exception is granted. Codes show limits: PA prior authorization, QL quantity limit, ST step therapy. Brand names are in capitals, generics in lowercase. The list can change during the year, so confirm on the Aetna member website or at 800-841-5374.

question: How much will my prescription cost?
expected_answer: Depends on the drug tier. For a 30-day supply: preferred generic $20, preferred brand $50, non-preferred generic or brand $75; no deductible. Insulin is capped at $25 per 30 days. Many birth control methods cost $0. If you ask for a brand when a generic exists, you also pay the price difference.

question: Which pharmacy should I use?
expected_answer: Any pharmacy in Aetna's network (more than 68,000, including CVS near campus). At an out-of-network pharmacy you pay full price and must file a claim.

question: The pharmacy says my drug needs prior authorization. What does that mean?
expected_answer: Aetna must approve the drug before it pays. Your doctor sends the request, usually online. Contact the doctor who prescribed it.

question: The pharmacy says my drug isn't covered. What can I do?
expected_answer: Ask your doctor for a covered alternative or a generic, or to request an exception. For a denial, contact the Insurance Navigators (215-746-4200).

question: Can I get a generic version to pay less?
expected_answer: Usually yes. Generics have the same active ingredients and meet the same FDA standards. Ask your doctor or pharmacist.

question: How do I refill my prescription?
expected_answer: Ask your pharmacy for a refill, or order through the Aetna member website. For drugs you take regularly, CVS Caremark Mail Service Pharmacy can mail up to a 90-day supply; order online or call 1-888-792-3862. Standard shipping is free.

question: What is an EOB?
expected_answer: An Explanation of Benefits is Aetna's statement of what the provider charged, what Aetna paid and what you may owe. It is not a bill.

question: What do the fields on my EOB mean?
expected_answer: Provider and date; amount billed (full charge); allowed amount (most Aetna pays); plan paid; patient responsibility (split into deductible, copay, coinsurance); remark codes explaining denials.

question: What does "patient responsibility" mean?
expected_answer: What you may owe after Aetna pays. Wait for the provider's bill and compare.

question: What does "applied to deductible" mean?
expected_answer: That amount counts toward your yearly deductible, so you pay it.

question: What's the difference between an EOB and a bill?
expected_answer: The EOB comes from Aetna and explains the claim. The bill comes from the provider and asks for payment.

question: Why does my EOB say "this is not a bill"?
expected_answer: Aetna is only reporting how it processed the claim. Pay only when the provider sends a bill.

question: Why did I get a bill when I thought Student Health was free?
expected_answer: The Clinical Fee covers most routine care, but some services, tests, medications or treatments, such as labs sent to an outside lab, are billed to insurance or cost extra.

question: Why was I charged for lab work done at Student Health?
expected_answer: The sample was taken at Student Health but tested by an outside lab, which billed your insurance. Your share is a $35 copay at an in-network lab, more at an out-of-network lab.

question: Why did I get a bill from a doctor I never met?
expected_answer: Hospitals often send separate bills for the building and for each doctor, such as a radiologist. The No Surprises Act limits out-of-network charges in emergencies and at in-network hospitals.

question: Why is my bill from Penn Medicine and not Aetna?
expected_answer: Providers send bills; Aetna does not. Penn Medicine bills you after Aetna processes the claim. Penn Medicine billing: 800-406-1177.

question: Who do I contact about a bill?
expected_answer: Start with the Insurance Navigators (215-746-4200, wel-shsinsur@pobox.upenn.edu). Claim questions: Aetna, 800-841-5374. Penn Medicine payment: 800-406-1177.

question: When should I contact the Insurance Navigators?
expected_answer: When a bill or EOB is confusing, a referral may have been missed, a claim was denied, or you don't know who to call. Office: 3535 Market St, Suite 60.

question: When should I call Aetna?
expected_answer: For claim status, what was paid, ID cards, adding dependents and finding in-network doctors: 800-841-5374.

question: When should I call the clinic's billing office?
expected_answer: To get an itemized bill, set up a payment plan, or check the claim was sent to Aetna correctly.

question: Can someone help me read my bill?
expected_answer: Yes: the Insurance Navigators, and Aetna's Personal Navigators through 800-841-5374.

question: I can't afford this bill. Is there help?
expected_answer: Ask the provider for a payment plan. For Penn Medicine bills, apply for financial assistance at 800-406-1177 or in MyChart; interpreters are available. Also contact the Insurance Navigators.

question: I'm sick while traveling in another US city. What do I do?
expected_answer: Use any Aetna in-network provider (find one in the Aetna Health app). No referral needed more than 25 miles from campus. Emergency: nearest ER.

question: Does PSIP cover me over the summer?
expected_answer: Yes, with annual coverage: August 1, 2026 to July 31, 2027. Spring-only coverage runs January 1 to July 31, 2027.

question: I'm going home to China. Am I covered there?
expected_answer: Yes. Care received outside the United States is paid at the in-network level; submit the claim with the provider's medical and payment details. On Call International helps with referrals and emergencies abroad (1-603-328-1956 collect).

question: I got care abroad. How do I get reimbursed?
expected_answer: Keep itemized bills and receipts, then file a claim form with Aetna (800-841-5374). Give Aetna written notice within 20 days and send the completed claim within 90 days of the care, or as soon as reasonably possible.

question: I'm on an internship in another state. How do I use my insurance?
expected_answer: Use Aetna in-network providers there; no referral is needed beyond 25 miles.

question: How do I get enough medication before going home?
expected_answer: Ask your doctor and pharmacy for a larger supply. In-network retail or mail order pharmacies can fill up to a 90-day supply ($60, $150 or $225 copay by tier); out-of-network pharmacies cannot fill more than 30 days. Birth control: up to 12 months. Lost or stolen prescriptions are not replaced.

question: I'm graduating. When does my coverage end?
expected_answer: Coverage runs to the end of the period you enrolled for, normally July 31. December graduates not returning in the spring: coverage ends January 31, 2027, and enrolled dependents' coverage ends with it.

question: Am I covered during OPT?
expected_answer: Not published. PSIP requires being registered in credit courses, so coverage likely ends with the period already paid for. Ask the Insurance Navigators and Penn ISSS.

question: What happens to my insurance if I take a leave of absence?
expected_answer: You can buy PSIP by asking the Insurance Navigators for an LOA Insurance application (215-746-WELL or wel-shsinsur@pobox.upenn.edu). No referrals needed while on leave.

question: Can my spouse or child use PSIP?
expected_answer: Yes, if you are enrolled first. Spouse or domestic partner (with a Penn Guest Card) and unmarried children under 26 who live with you. $5,018 per year each; $10,036 for two or more children; paid to Aetna. Newborns are covered 31 days and must be enrolled in that time.

question: My parents are visiting and one got sick. Are they covered?
expected_answer: No. Only enrolled students and enrolled spouses, partners and children are covered. Parents need their own travel insurance.

question: Does PSIP include vision or dental?
expected_answer: Limited. Eye exam: plan pays 90% in network, 1 per year, no referral; glasses or contacts up to $125 per year. Dental: only impacted wisdom teeth and injury to natural teeth, paid at 90%. Optional plans: Aetna Vision Preferred ($65 per year), Penn Student Dental Plan, Aetna Student Dental Plan ($395 per year).

question: What is the Vital Savings program?
expected_answer: An optional Aetna dental discount program. It is not insurance, and Penn Dental Family Practice does not accept it.

question: Does PSIP include travel assistance?
expected_answer: Aetna members get On Call International: 24/7 medical help abroad, emergency evacuation, translation, lost documents. Call 1-866-525-1956 (US/Canada) or 1-603-328-1956 collect. Penn's Aetna plan documents do not mention On Call International, so Penn's participation must be confirmed.

question: Can I ask you in Chinese (or Korean, Hindi, Spanish)?
expected_answer: Yes. The bot answers in your language and keeps insurance terms in English beside the translation.

question: Can you explain my EOB in my language?
expected_answer: Yes, field by field, with the English term shown. The bot does not judge whether the amounts are right.

question: Is there a Student Health doctor who speaks my language?
expected_answer: Not published. Ask Student Health at 215-746-WELL.

question: Can I get an interpreter? Does it cost anything?
expected_answer: At Penn Medicine hospitals and practices, interpreters are free in 140+ languages; ask when booking or call 800-789-7366. Aetna also offers free interpreters at 1-877-480-4161. Student Health and urgent care policies are not published.

question: Do the Insurance Navigators or Aetna offer help in my language?
expected_answer: Aetna: free interpreters and translated documents at 1-877-480-4161, or the number on your card. Insurance Navigators: not published.

question: Does CAPS have counselors who speak my language?
expected_answer: Not published. Ask Counseling at 215-898-7021.

question: How do I say "I have PSIP insurance" or "I need a referral" in English at the clinic?
expected_answer: "I have Aetna Student Health insurance through Penn." "I need a referral from Student Health to see a specialist." "Can I have an interpreter, please?"

question: What does "deductible" mean?
expected_answer: What you pay each year for covered care before insurance starts sharing costs. PSIP: $400 in network (with a referral) and $1,500 out of network (including care without a referral).

question: What's the difference between a copay and coinsurance?
expected_answer: A copay is a fixed amount per service (for example $30). Coinsurance is a percentage of the cost (for example 20%), usually after the deductible.

question: What is an "out-of-pocket maximum"?
expected_answer: The most you pay in a year for covered care; after that the plan pays 100%. Premiums don't count. PSIP: $1,500 per person in network, $4,000 out of network.

question: What do "in network" and "out of network" mean?
expected_answer: In network: providers with an Aetna contract, so you pay less. Out of network: no contract, so you pay more and may be balance billed.

question: What is "prior authorization"?
expected_answer: Approval from Aetna before certain services or drugs are covered. Your doctor asks for it.

question: What is a "referral"?
expected_answer: Written approval from your main doctor to see a specialist. For PSIP it comes from Student Health and lasts until July 31.

question: What does "allowed amount" mean on my EOB?
expected_answer: The most Aetna will pay a provider for a service.

question: What do "claim," "denial" and "appeal" mean?
expected_answer: Claim: a request to Aetna to pay for care. Denial: Aetna refusing to pay. Appeal: asking Aetna to reconsider a denial (get help from the Insurance Navigators).

question: What is a "premium"?
expected_answer: What you pay to have insurance, even if you don't use care. PSIP: $5,018 for 2026–27.

question: What are a "formulary" and "drug tiers"?
expected_answer: The formulary is the list of covered drugs. Tiers are cost levels; higher tiers cost more.

question: What does "balance billing" mean?
expected_answer: When an out-of-network provider bills you the difference between its price and what Aetna allows. Limited by the No Surprises Act in emergencies.

question: What does "PPO" mean?
expected_answer: Preferred Provider Organization: you can see in- or out-of-network providers, but in network costs less. PSIP is an Aetna PPO plus a Student Health referral rule.
